q: What are the finishing tools on the node grader?
a: Finishing touches after a grade: film grain (a little grain makes shots feel alike and hides banding in smooth gradients), highlight soft clip for skies and lamps that clip, a LUT on a node for a camera conversion or a look, and a final check with the scopes.

q: What should I do once the grade itself is done?
a: Finishing touches after a grade: film grain (a little grain makes shots feel alike and hides banding in smooth gradients), highlight soft clip for skies and lamps that clip, a LUT on a node for a camera conversion or a look, and a final check with the scopes.

q: Where are the film grain controls?
a: Grain is in the Primaries panel, in the Film grain group below the other sliders, and belongs to the selected node (its box then reads Grain). Grain strength 0 to 1 (0 is off) sets how visible; Grain size 1 to 4 is the cell size in the clip's source pixels; Grain softness 0 to 1 (0.5) goes from crisp to smooth. The ↺ buttons go back to neutral.

q: How do I reset grain to off?
a: Grain is in the Primaries panel, in the Film grain group below the other sliders, and belongs to the selected node (its box then reads Grain). q: Will the grain look the same in the export as in the viewer?
a: Yes: the grain is different on every frame, but the same frame always gets the same grain, so an export matches the viewer. It is monochrome and weighted by brightness.

q: In Resolve I'd use the Film Grain effect. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Use a node's own grain: select a last node for the look (or + Serial), raise Grain strength slowly (0.1 to 0.2), set Grain size at 100 percent view. Here grain is a setting of a node, not a separate plugin.

q: In Premiere I'd add a Noise effect for grain. What's better here?
a: Use a node's own grain: select a last node for the look (or + Serial), raise Grain strength slowly (0.1 to 0.2), set Grain size at 100 percent view. Here grain is a setting of a node, not a separate plugin.

q: What does highlight roll-off do?
a: Highlight soft clip bends the brightest part of the picture down smoothly so highlights keep some shape instead of clipping flat. On a late node open the Curves tab: under Soft clip raise Highlight roll-off (0 off, 1 full) and set Roll-off knee where the bending starts, on a display-like scale where 1 is diffuse white (0.5 starts in the upper mid-tones, 0.95 only touches the brightest highlights). Scripts use `hl.rolloff`, `hl.knee` with `grade.setParam`.

q: Does soft clip replace the output tone mapping?
a: No: the sequence's output stage still applies its own BT.2390 tone mapping afterwards. Soft clip is a per-node look tool; at full roll-off brightness approaches diffuse white smoothly and never passes it.

q: In Resolve I'd use Soft Clip. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Use Highlight roll-off and Roll-off knee under Soft clip in a node's Curves tab. Unlike Resolve there's no low (shadow) soft clip and no per-channel setting.

q: In Premiere I'd pull down Lumetri Whites. What's the node grader way?
a: Use Highlight roll-off and Roll-off knee under Soft clip in a node's Curves tab. Unlike Resolve there's no low (shadow) soft clip and no per-channel setting.

q: Which LUT file formats can I load?
a: A LUT is a ready-made colour transform in a file: a camera conversion, a film-print emulation or a show look. On a node it sits after the node's own corrections and later nodes can still adjust it. Select the node, open the LUT menu at the bottom of the Primaries tab and pick a built-in LUT, one from the project's LUT library, or Browse… for a `.cube` / `.3dl` file (copied into the project, `lut.import`); the command is `grade.setLut`. LUT mix blends it; None removes it.

q: How do I remove a LUT from a node?

q: In Premiere I'd load a Creative Look LUT in Lumetri. How do I do that on a node?
a: Select the node and use the LUT menu at the bottom of the Primaries tab, with LUT mix to blend it. The LUT works on the node's grading signal (DaVinci Intermediate in a DaVinci Wide Gamut sequence), so use a LUT made for that signal, or put a conversion before it.

q: What does the waveform show?
a: The waveform shows the brightness of every column of the picture, left to right, bottom black, top white. For exposure: blacks just above the bottom (Lift), highlights just below the top (Gain), faces roughly in the middle (Gamma).

q: Where should blacks and highlights sit on the waveform?
a: The waveform shows the brightness of every column of the picture, left to right, bottom black, top white. For exposure: blacks just above the bottom (Lift), highlights just below the top (Gain), faces roughly in the middle (Gamma).

q: What's the difference between the YUV and HLS vectorscope?
a: Both show hue as the angle and saturation as the distance from the centre. Vectorscope YUV is the one to check skin (along the skin-tone line) and spot casts (a neutral shot clusters in the centre); Vectorscope HLS has hue labels round the circle, handy to name a cast by its hue.

q: How do I name a colour cast?
a: Both show hue as the angle and saturation as the distance from the centre. Vectorscope YUV is the one to check skin (along the skin-tone line) and spot casts (a neutral shot clusters in the centre); Vectorscope HLS has hue labels round the circle, handy to name a cast by its hue.

q: How do I choose which scopes are shown?
a: Click the wrench (or right-click the scopes) and tick the scopes you want, e.g. Waveform and Parade, unticking others to give them room. The bottom bar picks the colour space (Automatic follows the sequence) and the scale: 8 Bit, Float or HDR. Agents read the same numbers with `scopes.read`.

q: In Resolve I use the scope viewer. Are the scopes here the same?
a: They're one Lumetri Scopes panel with several scopes side by side, as in Premiere; on the Color page open it from the page toolbar. The readings mean the same as Resolve's: Waveform, Parade, Vectorscope and Histogram map one to one.

q: and the parade, what should it look like on a white shirt?
a: On something white or grey the red, green and blue traces of the parade should sit at the same height. If one is higher, correct it with Temperature / Tint or the wheels.
